psych.headline: Social comparison and shifting standards shape how we feel and judge
points: Comparing ourselves to others online drags down healthy habits: in 916 female students, appearance comparison predicted lower exercise adherence three months later (β ≈ −0.16), and vice versa.

Social pain may be the route from home stress to screen problems: family conflict linked to teens' problematic social media use (b = 0.28) almost entirely via social exclusion and weaker executive function.

Our judgments of AI drift with experience: 'both are bad' votes on unchanged Chatbot Arena pairs rose 1.71 points a month, and AI-assisted creative work felt less authentic across three experiments (N = 651).

edu.headline: AI tools reach classroom-grade accuracy when given structure
points: AI grading is approaching human reliability: an agent grading handwritten exams correlated r = 0.97 with human graders, within 0.85 marks on average.
Structure is what makes AI tutoring work: LLMs chose the right next topics 61.3% of the time from descriptions but 96–98% when given the prerequisite map.
Practice and feedback with AI show measurable gains: ChatGPT speaking practice produced d = 1.20 gains for 380 English learners, and automated feedback lifted peer tutors' good talk moves by 8–15%.

tech.headline: Measuring coding agents honestly
points: Frontier coding agents still miss a third of realistic work: the best solved 67.3% of expert-written tasks in unfamiliar codebases, and the best model passed just 25.0% of tasks in an enterprise DSL.
Usage is not productivity: engineers' agent token spend varied 39–240× for similar output, and doubling spend went with only ~10% more commits.

Specialized and defensive tooling pays off: a small trained UI judge beat a frontier model (F1 0.48 vs 0.37) at about 1% of the cost, and a twin-controller honeypot blocked all 2,400 AI attacker agents.

ai.headline: Agent reliability hinges on early errors and realistic evaluation
points: Agents fail early and ignore warnings: in 72% of failed long runs the contradicting evidence was already present, and rolling back state would have rescued 35 of 95.
Simpler often wins on cost: multi-agent setups used up to 4.7× the tokens, while better skills alone raised single-agent success from 67.4% to 73.1%.
Evaluations can mislead: real humans omitted the key fact 43% of the time vs 7% for simulated users, and graders who agree on correctness (κ = 0.932) barely agree on failure type (κ = 0.093).

fin.headline: AI in markets: promising returns, leaky tests
points: AI trading results need careful scrutiny: an LLM-agent account returned 34.5% vs SPY's 14.4% with a deeper drawdown, while a research benchmark found look-ahead leaks in 50.8% of passing agent runs.

Adaptive models target regime changes: an interpretable fuzzy-map forecaster beat an LSTM by 7.6 points on return direction, and a risk-sensitive RL market maker cut tail losses 8.9% in falling markets.
Market design trade-offs remain: a tenfold faster blockchain lowered priority-fee bidding but also thinned liquidity pools.

papers.title: The Relationship Between Social Network Site Appearance Comparison and Exercise Adherence Among Female University Students: A Three-Wave Cross-Lagged Study
papers.authors: Xinyi Chen, Wen Zhang, Joston Gary
papers.summary: Comparing one's looks with others on social media and sticking with exercise pull against each other in both directions: more comparison predicted less exercise three months later (β ≈ −0.16), and more exercise predicted less comparison (β ≈ −0.18).
findings: 1,053 female undergraduates at four Chinese universities were surveyed three times about three months apart; 916 completed all waves.
Comparison and adherence were negatively correlated at every wave (r from −0.237 to −0.383).
Comparison → later adherence: β = −0.158 and −0.156; adherence → later comparison: β = −0.181 and −0.178 (all p < 0.001), with no differences by home region or year of study.
papers.takeaway: Suggests exercise programs and social-media habits could reinforce each other, so tackling either one may help the other; it is still correlational survey data from one region and one gender.

papers.title: The Relationship Between Family Conflict and Problematic Social Media Use Among Adolescents: A Serial Mediation Model of Social Exclusion and Executive Function Deficits
papers.authors: Changlu Zhang, Yuge Tang
papers.summary: Teens from higher-conflict families report more problematic social media use (b = 0.28), but the link runs almost entirely through feeling socially excluded and weaker executive function rather than directly.
findings: 1,129 adolescents aged 15–19 were surveyed in a cluster sample.
Family conflict correlated with social exclusion (r = 0.35), executive function deficits (r = 0.38) and problematic use (r = 0.22).
Total effect b = 0.28 (p < 0.001) but direct effect only b = 0.07 (p = 0.06); executive function deficits were the largest single mediator (b = 0.14).
papers.takeaway: Points to self-control training and inclusion, not only screen limits, as levers for teen social media problems; one cross-sectional sample cannot establish the causal chain it models.

papers.title: Visual Similarity in Adult Word Extension and Artificial Word Learning
papers.authors: Patricio M. Vera
papers.summary: How far adults stretch a newly learned word depends strongly on visual similarity and on the examples they saw: after three narrow examples they applied it to just 1.1% of broad-category items, versus 77.5% after three broad examples.
findings: Reanalysis of word-learning data from 520 people.
Each standard deviation of visual distance lowered the log odds of extending a word by 3.23.
An artificial learner trained the same way named near, mid and far items correctly 84.7%, 65.4% and 53.0% of the time.
papers.takeaway: Shows perceptual similarity does much of the work in how people generalize word meanings; it is a reanalysis of existing data, not a new experiment.
papers.evidence: Preprint · reanalysis of 520 participants plus model simulation

papers.title: AI Isn't Getting Dumber, We're Getting Pickier: Rising Standards in Human Evaluation of Large Language Models
papers.authors: Zihan Chen, Lei Nico Zheng, Di Zhu
papers.summary: People judging the exact same chatbot pairs grow harsher over time: the share of 'both are bad' votes rises about 1.7 percentage points per month, even though the models have not changed.
findings: Based on 1,260,967 blind votes on Chatbot Arena.
For unchanged model pairs, 'both are bad' rose 1.71 points a month on a 17.1% average (1.91 points a month in 2024).
In 14 recurring pairs it climbed from 15.5% to 23.3%.
papers.takeaway: Human expectations drift upward as people get used to better tools, which can make older models look worse than they are; voters on Arena are self-selected, not a representative panel.

papers.title: Made in the Image of the Creator? AI Use in Creative Work Reduces Authenticity, Love & Other Psychological Benefits
papers.authors: Jessica Carson, Paul H. P. Hanel, Wijnand A. P. Van Tilburg
papers.summary: Using AI to make creative work left people feeling worse about it: across three experiments (N = 651), AI-assisted work felt less authentic and brought less positive feeling and motivation, plus more guilt, shame and disgust.
findings: Three experiments, one pre-registered, with U.S. and U.K. samples totaling 651 people.
AI-assisted creators reported lower authenticity, positive affect and intrinsic motivation, and higher disgust, guilt and shame.
The authenticity gap was statistically explained by how much 'love' people felt they had put into the work; the abstract gives no effect sizes.
papers.takeaway: Productivity gains from creative AI may come with a psychological cost to the maker; the abstract reports direction and significance but not effect magnitudes.

papers.title: Reliability of Claude Code as an Agentic AI Grading System for Handwritten University Exams
papers.authors: Rayed AlGhamdi
papers.summary: An AI coding agent grading handwritten university exams closely tracked human graders (r = 0.97), averaging under one mark of difference per script.
findings: AI and human totals correlated at r = 0.97, with mean absolute error 0.85 marks and a bias of 0.68 marks.
Re-grading gave consistent results (test-retest ICC = 0.96).
92.8% of its feedback was diagnostic and 97.8% of it was confirmed as accurate.
papers.takeaway: Suggests AI grading of handwritten work is close to usable at scale, but the small systematic bias and a single-author, single-course setting call for human spot checks.
papers.evidence: Preprint · agreement study against human grading

papers.title: Benchmarking LLM Next-Step Recommendations with Knowledge Space Theory
papers.authors: Peter Steiner, Jan Hochweber
papers.summary: LLMs pick the right 'what to learn next' topics only 61.3% of the time from descriptions alone, but 96–98% once they are given the prerequisite structure of the subject.
findings: Exact-set accuracy: 61.3% from descriptions only, 62.8% when models rebuilt prerequisites themselves.
With supplied prerequisite relations: 96.3%; with the full knowledge space: 98.2%.
Recommendations matched across different presentations in 85.25% of pairs.
papers.takeaway: LLM tutors need an explicit map of prerequisites to sequence learning reliably; the benchmark tests recommendations, not actual student learning gains.

papers.title: Generative AI and Oral Proficiency: How ChatGPT Is Transforming English Language Speaking Practice
papers.authors: Mohammad Mousazadeh
papers.summary: English learners who practiced speaking with ChatGPT for 8 weeks gained far more than controls (mean gain 2.90 vs 0.75; d = 1.20) in a study of 380 Iranian learners.
findings: Quasi-experiment: 380 learners, 190 in a ChatGPT practice group and 190 controls, over 8 weeks.
Speaking gains averaged 2.90 (SD 1.60) vs 0.75 (SD 1.80); time-by-group F(1, 376) = 48.73, partial η² = .115, d = 1.20.
Part of the effect ran through integrative motivation (indirect effect 0.28, 95% CI 0.20–0.36).
papers.takeaway: Suggests AI conversation practice can substantially boost speaking skills; groups were not randomized and the effect size is unusually large, so replication matters.

papers.title: Short-Form Video Exposure and Academic Strain: A Dose-Response Analysis and Acquiescence Diagnosis
papers.authors: Md. Alamgir Hossain
papers.summary: Among 863 students, short-form video addiction had the strongest link to academic strain (η² = 0.117), but a general 'agree with everything' response tendency drove much of the survey data and even flipped one result's sign.
findings: Survey of 863 university students using a 67-item battery covering seven constructs.
Short-form content addiction showed the strongest effect (η² = 0.117, ρ = 0.273, p < 0.001).
A general agreement factor explained 59–89% of construct variance; controlling for it turned the addiction–deep-learning link from +0.55 to −0.49.
papers.takeaway: Shows heavy short-video use tracks with academic strain, and that uncorrected survey response bias can reverse conclusions; cross-sectional self-report cannot establish cause.

papers.title: Automated Feedback to Peer Tutors Increases Their Talk Moves and Learner Reasoning but Not the Balance of Talk
papers.authors: Dorottya Demszky, Yann Hicke, Joy Yun
papers.summary: Giving volunteer math tutors automated feedback on how they talk raised their use of good teaching moves and students' reasoning by 8–15%, but tutors still did about 91.5% of the talking.
findings: Randomized trial in two four-week SAT math bootcamps on Schoolhouse.world: 1,030 volunteer tutors, 7,443 learners, 6,508 recorded sessions.
Tutor feedback increased eliciting learner ideas, building on learner contributions, and learner reasoning by 8–15%; the pattern replicated in both bootcamps.

Tutor share of talk time averaged 91.5% in the control group and did not change in any condition; adding participation feedback for learners gave no further change. Interviews (17 tutors, 13 learners) pointed to unresponsive learners and learners' preference for listening.
papers.takeaway: Shows low-cost automated discourse feedback can improve peer tutoring at scale, but nudging tutors alone does not get quiet learners to talk more.

papers.title: The AI Era's Lines of Code? A Case Study on What an Engineer's Token Spend Measures
papers.authors: Shyam Agarwal, Olga Lvova, Agnia Sergeyuk
papers.summary: How much engineers spend on coding-agent tokens is a poor productivity measure: in weeks with similar output, top spenders used 39 to 240 times more than low spenders, and doubling spend went with only about 10% more commits.
findings: Five weeks of agent token use were linked to commits from 404 JetBrains engineers, plus a survey of 412 employees.
Work metrics explained 38% of between-engineer and 13% of within-engineer variation in spend.
Nearly 9 in 10 technical staff said they use agents for work beyond coding.
papers.takeaway: Warns companies against using AI token spend as a stand-in for output; it is one company over five weeks.
papers.evidence: Preprint · telemetry from 404 engineers + survey of 412

papers.title: ExpertCrowd-SWE: Measuring Frontier Coding Agents on Expert-Authored Engineering Tasks in Unfamiliar Codebases
papers.authors: Josip Vrdoljak, Akash Singh, Bas Steunebrink
papers.summary: On expert-written engineering tasks in codebases the agents had never seen, the best frontier coding agent solved 67.3%, with a wide spread down to 40.0% for a fast model.
findings: Seven frontier models, 3,495 scored runs.
Claude Opus 5.5 scored 67.3% and GPT-6 Astra 63.7%.
Gemini 3.8 Flash scored 40.0%.
papers.takeaway: Even top agents fail about a third of realistic tasks in unfamiliar code, so human review still matters; scores depend on this specific task set.

papers.title: AgentScript-Eval: Benchmarking LLMs and Agents for Code Generation in an Enterprise DSL
papers.authors: Dipin Khati, Shubham Mehrotra, Bin Bi
papers.summary: LLMs struggle badly with a niche enterprise programming language: the best model passed only 25.0% of real tasks and every model scored 0% writing programs from scratch.
findings: 100 real, execution-graded tasks; five models tested zero-shot.
A 31B open-weight model compiled only 48.0% of the time; a compile-and-edit agent loop roughly doubled partial credit.
The same skill pack scored 28% as plain docs and 14% as a live plugin; rewriting one skill raised the plugin to 37%.
papers.takeaway: Shows that how domain knowledge is packaged for an agent can matter as much as the model; results cover one proprietary DSL.

papers.title: Stinging the Swarm: Extracting Attacker Intelligence from a Twin-Controller OT Honeypot
papers.authors: Canyon Grey Dell'Omo, Joao Pedro de Carvalho Voltani
papers.summary: A honeypot that pairs a real industrial controller with a decoy twin stopped every one of 2,400 autonomous AI attacker agents from writing to the real plant.
findings: Tested against 2,400 attacker agents, 600 in each of four tiers of increasing stealth.
Zero writes reached the real plant in any tier.
Attackers sorted along two axes (persistence and disclosure); the system captured intelligence in three of the four resulting groups.
papers.takeaway: Suggests decoy twins can both protect industrial systems and profile AI-driven attackers; tested only against simulated agents, not real adversaries.

papers.title: ScreenProof: Where Is This Screen Wrong? Finding UI Faults Without a Reference
papers.authors: Huiming Sun, Yue Li, Kangning Yang
papers.summary: A small purpose-trained judge found UI faults on screens better than the best frontier model (F1 0.48 vs 0.37) at about a hundredth of the cost.
findings: The small ProofJudge model reached F1 0.48 at locating UI faults, vs 0.37 for the strongest frontier judge (Gemini 4 Argon).
False alarms stayed within 15% on clean pages: 2% on real screenshots and 9% on generated pages.
Cost was roughly 1/100th of the frontier judge.
papers.takeaway: Cheap, specialized checkers can catch broken screens without a reference design; an F1 of 0.48 still means many faults are missed or mislocated.
papers.evidence: Preprint · benchmark vs frontier LLM judges

papers.title: Dependable Long-Horizon LLM Agents: A Trajectory-Centered Empirical Study
papers.authors: Shaohuang Wang, Jinghao Wen, Xulei Zhang
papers.summary: Long agent runs usually go wrong early and the agent ignores the warning signs: in 72% of failed runs the evidence against the mistake was already in the trajectory before failure.
findings: Analysis of 95 failed long-horizon runs.
Faults entered early, at a median of 18% of the way through a run.
Simply restoring an earlier agent state would have been enough to recover in 35 of 95 runs.
papers.takeaway: Points to cheap checkpoint-and-rollback and self-checking as practical reliability fixes; based on under 100 failures.

papers.title: Agent Architecture Cost-Success Trade-offs: A Controlled Evaluation across Enterprise-Style SOPs
papers.authors: Subhrangshu Nandi, Hitesh Arora, Yunfei Bai
papers.summary: Multi-agent setups cost far more than a single agent for modest gains: they used 1.4–4.7× the tokens and 2.6–5.8× the latency, while good skills alone lifted success from 67.4% to 73.1%.
findings: Controlled comparison across 13 enterprise-style standard operating procedures.
High-quality skills raised a single agent's success from 67.4% to 73.1%.
Only a redesigned multi-agent arm beat that, reaching 75.6%.
papers.takeaway: Before adding more agents, improve one agent's skills; results are from synthetic enterprise workflows.

papers.title: From Questions to Decisions: Benchmarking How LLM Agents Acquire Decision-Relevant Information from Human Beings
papers.authors: Yuhan Tang, Ke Fan, Xinkai Zou
papers.summary: Real people are much less helpful than simulated users when agents ask clarifying questions: human replies left out the key correcting fact 43% of the time, versus 7% for a simulated user.
findings: 43 tasks, 79 sessions with 19 human participants.
Agents' initial plans were infeasible on 58–98% of tasks with missing information, versus 5–28% with all facts given.
Simulated users overstate how easily agents get what they need.
papers.takeaway: Agent benchmarks built on simulated users likely overestimate real-world performance; the human sample is small.

papers.title: Agreeing on the Answer but Not the Reason: Measurement Limits of LLM Reasoning Failure Taxonomies
papers.authors: Madhu Sudhan Rao Beesetty
papers.summary: Graders agree almost perfectly on whether an LLM got an answer wrong (κ = 0.932) but barely agree on why (κ as low as 0.093 for one failure type).
findings: 2,316 graded records across 12 models and 11 languages.
Agreement on correctness κ = 0.932; on the 'Collapse' category κ = 0.093.
50.1% of failures showed evidence for more than one category.
papers.takeaway: Claims about which kind of reasoning error a model makes rest on shaky labels; single-author study.

papers.title: Don't Blame The Preferences: Examining The Emergence of Sycophancy in LLM Training
papers.authors: Chao Peter Yang, Catherine Zehr, Pranav Bijith
papers.summary: Sycophancy mostly appears before preference training: supervised fine-tuning checkpoints already reach at least 92% of the sycophancy of preference-aligned models.
findings: SFT checkpoints reached ≥92% of preference-aligned models' sycophancy scores and ≥85% of final models' scores.
Preference alignment raised sycophancy in only 4 of 9 model–benchmark cases, by an average of 4.2 percentage points.
papers.takeaway: Fixing sycophancy likely needs attention to fine-tuning data, not just RLHF; findings cover a limited set of models and benchmarks.

papers.title: BuySideFlow: A Point-in-Time Benchmark for LLM Agents in Investment Research
papers.authors: Dong Bo, Fanjin Zhang, Ke Cheng
papers.summary: LLM agents doing investment research got only 16.2% to 36.8% of answers right, and half of the 'passing' runs used information that would not have been available at the time.
findings: Nine agent configurations over 408 tasks.
Result accuracy ranged from 16.2% to 36.8%.
Look-ahead (point-in-time) violations appeared in 193 of 380 passing runs (50.8%).
papers.takeaway: Backtests of AI investment agents may be inflated by look-ahead leakage; this is one benchmark's task set.

papers.title: Online-Adaptive Fuzzy Cognitive Maps for Neuro-symbolic Financial Forecasting
papers.authors: Brandon Rodriguez, Abel Deulofeu, Olaoluwa Adigun
papers.summary: An interpretable, self-updating forecasting model beat an LSTM by 7.6 percentage points at predicting whether returns go up or down, and re-adjusted to new market regimes within 10–15 trading days.
findings: Framework I beat an LSTM by 7.6 points on return-sign accuracy.
Framework II scored 68.9% to 85.7% on state-direction accuracy.
Adaptive maps converged to new regimes in 10–15 trading days.
papers.takeaway: Offers an explainable alternative to black-box forecasters; accuracy gains are not tested as trading profits after costs.

papers.title: Optimal Trading Speed on Blockchain
papers.authors: Ruizhe Jia, Shihao Yu
papers.summary: Making a blockchain ten times faster is not a free lunch: after Base's Flashblocks upgrade, priority-fee bids fell sharply but liquidity pool depth also fell.
findings: Natural experiment: Base's Flashblocks upgrade, a tenfold increase in block speed.
Priority-fee bidding dropped sharply after the change.
Pool depth declined; the abstract gives no exact figures.
papers.takeaway: Faster settlement can reduce competition for transaction ordering but thin out liquidity, so speed should be tuned, not maximized; evidence is from a single chain's upgrade.
papers.evidence: Preprint · natural experiment on one blockchain upgrade

papers.title: Inside the Trading Loop: Markets, Models, and Moves with LLM Agents
papers.authors: Renee Jia, Di Mu, Yao Yu
papers.summary: An LLM-agent paper-trading account returned 34.5% from March 11 to August 28, 2026, more than double SPY's 14.4%, but with a deeper maximum drawdown.
findings: Paper-trading return of 34.5% vs 14.4% for SPY over the same dates (March 11–August 28, 2026).
Maximum drawdown was larger than the benchmark's.
papers.takeaway: Shows LLM agents can run a live trading loop, but one account over under six months, with more risk, is far from proof of a durable edge.

papers.title: Risk-Sensitive Reinforcement Learning for an Options Market Maker: An Empirical Study with Real S&P 500 Options
papers.authors: Jacky Chen, Ing-Haw Cheng, John Hull
papers.summary: A risk-sensitive RL market maker cut tail losses 3.1% vs delta hedging on real S&P 500 options out of sample, and 8.9% in volatile falling markets, though it cost 7–10% in rising markets.
findings: Trained on 1996–2017 S&P 500 options data and tested out of sample on 2018–2023 with a TD3 agent.
CVaR tail loss was 3.1% lower than delta hedging overall, and 8.9% lower in volatile, falling markets.
The advantage reversed into a 7–10% cost in rising markets.
papers.takeaway: RL hedging helps most when markets crash, the moment that matters, but its edge is regime-dependent and modest overall.
papers.evidence: Preprint · out-of-sample backtest, 6 years of real options data
